Welcome to 6th Grade Digital Discoveries

CPALMS #0200021 Florida CS Standards SC.6.*

Optima Academy Online — Grade 6 Digital Discoveries (CPALMS #0200021). An asynchronous, self-paced computer science course aligned to Florida Computer Science Standards (SC.6.*). Students explore digital communication, data and cyber safety, programming with Python, modeling and AI ethics, and complete a year-end capstone project.

What you'll learn this year

Across five units and 36 weeks, you'll move from everyday digital communication into the fundamentals of programming, modeling, and AI ethics — finishing with a year-end capstone where you put it all together.

Course flow

  • Unit 1 — Digital Foundations — Weeks 1–7. Digital communication, multimedia, file organization, productivity tools.
  • Unit 2 — Data & Cyber Safety — Weeks 9–18. The journey of data, permissions, phishing, encryption, source evaluation, and digital wellness.
  • Unit 3 — Programming — Weeks 19–28. Computational thinking, flowcharts, Python data types, conditionals, loops, functions, debugging.
  • Unit 4 — Modeling, Design & AI — Weeks 29–33. Simulation, the engineering design process, AI fundamentals, ethics, and human-AI collaboration.
  • Unit 5 — Capstone & Course Final — Weeks 35–36. Careers in computing, year-end capstone project, and course final.

How each week works

  • Reading — the concept page introducing the week's topic and vocabulary.
  • Activity — an interactive practice task (scenarios, sorting, decision-making) that reinforces the reading.
  • Quiz — 5 multiple-choice questions, 3 attempts, instant feedback. Best attempt is kept.

At the end of each unit, a longer summative Unit Assessment checks your mastery. Unit 5 ends with the cumulative Course Final.

Getting started

  1. Click Modules in the left sidebar — that's the main navigation for this course.
  2. Open the Course Syllabus page (in the Start Here module) to see the full week-by-week plan.
  3. Start with Unit 1, Week 1 and complete each week's reading → activity → quiz in order.

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST example of synchronous digital communication?

answers.text: Posting a reply to a discussion board the night before class
answers.feedback: ❌ Discussion posts are asynchronous — they're read whenever the reader gets to them, not in real time.

answers.text: Sending an email to your teacher about homework
answers.feedback: ❌ Email is asynchronous — the sender and receiver are not online at the same time.

answers.text: Joining a live video class with your teacher and classmates
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Live video calls are synchronous: everyone is present and communicating in real time. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: Leaving a voicemail for a friend
answers.feedback: ❌ A voicemail is asynchronous — the friend listens to it later, not while you speak.

questions.text: What is a data packet?

answers.text: A folder that stores all of your digital files
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes storage or a directory, not a data packet.

answers.text: A password that protects your messages
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes encryption or authentication, not a data packet.

answers.text: A small chunk of information that travels across a network
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Data packets are small pieces of a larger message that travel separately across a network and are reassembled at the destination. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: A type of router used to connect devices
answers.feedback: ❌ Routers direct packets — they aren't packets themselves.

questions.text: You need to send a detailed question to your science teacher about an upcoming project. Which tool is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: A quick text message with abbreviations
answers.feedback: ❌ A text with abbreviations is too informal for a teacher — the tone won't match the audience.

answers.text: An email written in a clear, polite tone
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Email is asynchronous, professional, and leaves a written record — ideal for a detailed question to a teacher. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: A reaction emoji on a class post
answers.feedback: ❌ A single emoji can't carry a full question. The teacher won't know what you're asking.

answers.text: A live video call at midnight
answers.feedback: ❌ Synchronous calls require both people present — and late-night timing isn't appropriate for a teacher.

questions.text: Which statement BEST describes asynchronous communication?

answers.text: Both people must be online at the same time to communicate
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes synchronous, not asynchronous. The prefix "a-" means "not" — asynchronous means NOT together in time.

answers.text: Messages are sent and received at different times, not in real time
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Asynchronous = not together in time. Emails and discussion posts are classic examples. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: Asynchronous communication only works for video calls
answers.feedback: ❌ Video calls are typically synchronous, which is the opposite of asynchronous.

answers.text: Asynchronous communication requires a special kind of network
answers.feedback: ❌ Asynchronous tools use the same networks as synchronous ones. The difference is in timing, not hardware.

questions.text: In digital communication, what is the role of a router?

answers.text: It creates new messages on behalf of the sender
answers.feedback: ❌ Routers don't write messages — they move them.

answers.text: It stores all data packets permanently on a server
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes storage or archiving, not routing.

answers.text: It directs data packets to the correct destination across a network
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A router is like a digital traffic cop — it reads each packet's destination and sends it along the fastest route. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: It converts text messages into voice messages
answers.feedback: ❌ That's voice-to-text software — not a router.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Quiz — Digital Communication in Practice

questions.text: What does the word "netiquette" mean?

answers.text: A special kind of internet connection
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes hardware or network speed — not a behavior rule.

answers.text: The unwritten rules of respectful online communication
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! "Netiquette" blends "network" and "etiquette" — it's the code of polite online conduct. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: A software that blocks bad messages
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes a filter or moderation tool, not netiquette.

answers.text: The name of a popular social media app
answers.feedback: ❌ Netiquette isn't an app — it's a set of behavior norms.

questions.text: The 3 C's of effective digital writing are:

answers.text: Creativity, caution, curiosity
answers.feedback: ❌ Good qualities, but not the 3 C's of digital writing.

answers.text: Color, contrast, clarity
answers.feedback: ❌ Clarity is correct, but color and contrast belong to visual design, not writing.

answers.text: Clarity, concision, courtesy
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Clarity (be understood), concision (respect the reader's time), courtesy (kind tone). (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: Confidence, charm, cleverness
answers.feedback: ❌ These sound nice, but they are not the 3 C's of digital writing.

questions.text: You just wrote an angry reply to a discussion post. What is the WISEST action?

answers.text: Save it as a draft, wait at least 30 minutes, and reread it before sending
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! This is the virtue of temperance in action — pausing before reacting. If the message still fits after the break, send. If not, you saved yourself. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: Post it right away while you still feel strongly about it
answers.feedback: ❌ Messages written in strong emotion almost always sound worse the next day. This breaks the virtue of temperance.

answers.text: Send it privately to a few friends first
answers.feedback: ❌ Now multiple people have a copy they could share. Not a safer path — a riskier one.

answers.text: Type it in ALL CAPS so your point is clear
answers.feedback: ❌ ALL CAPS reads like shouting and breaks netiquette — this makes the problem worse, not better.

questions.text: Which version of "I can't make practice today" has the BEST tone for a teacher or coach?

answers.text: "cant come 2 practice, sry"
answers.feedback: ❌ Too casual and abbreviated for a teacher or coach. The tone doesn't fit the audience.

answers.text: "WHY DOES EVERYONE THINK I CAN COME TO EVERYTHING"
answers.feedback: ❌ ALL CAPS = shouting. Tone is also accusatory, not respectful.

answers.text: "Hi Coach, I won't be able to attend practice today due to a family commitment. I'll be there Wednesday. Thank you."
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Formal, respectful, specific — tone matches the audience. Includes greeting, reason, plan, and thanks. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: "not coming today 🙃"
answers.feedback: ❌ Too curt and too casual. Missing greeting, reason, and any courtesy for a coach or teacher.

questions.text: The classical virtue of prudence, applied to digital communication, means:

answers.text: Being brave enough to post your real opinions
answers.feedback: ❌ That's closer to fortitude (courage), not prudence.

answers.text: Wisely choosing the right action at the right moment — the right tool, audience, and timing
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Prudence is practical wisdom. Online, it's asking "Is this the right channel? Right time? Right audience?" before acting. (SC.6.CC.1.1)

answers.text: Treating every person fairly and equally
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes the virtue of justice — important, but a different virtue.

answers.text: Staying calm when you're angry
answers.feedback: ❌ Close! That's temperance (self-control), not prudence (wise choice). Prudence decides; temperance restrains.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Quiz — Introduction to Multimedia Design

questions.text: What does "multimedia" mean?

answers.text: Content that uses only video
answers.feedback: ❌ Video alone is one medium. Multimedia means MORE than one type combined.

answers.text: Content that uses only audio
answers.feedback: ❌ Audio alone is one medium. Multimedia combines two or more types on purpose.

answers.text: Content that combines two or more types of media (text, images, audio, video) on purpose
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! "Multi-" means "many." Multimedia is many media types working together. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Content that uses only text
answers.feedback: ❌ Text alone is one medium. The whole point of multimedia is combining types.

questions.text: The three classical rhetorical purposes of communication — first identified by Aristotle — are:

answers.text: Inform, confuse, frustrate
answers.feedback: ❌ "Confuse" and "frustrate" aren't real rhetorical purposes — and good designers avoid both!

answers.text: Inform, persuade, entertain
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Aristotle's framework, still used today: teach (inform), change what people think or do (persuade), or delight (entertain). (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Type, click, scroll
answers.feedback: ❌ Those are user actions, not communication purposes.

answers.text: Sketch, code, present
answers.feedback: ❌ Those are creative steps, not rhetorical purposes.

questions.text: You're designing a slideshow for kindergarten students. Which choice shows the BEST audience awareness?

answers.text: Long paragraphs of text on every slide
answers.feedback: ❌ Kindergarteners can't read paragraphs. Wrong audience.

answers.text: A 20-page report with footnotes
answers.feedback: ❌ Reports with footnotes fit a college audience, not 5-year-olds.

answers.text: Big, friendly images and one short sentence per slide
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Audience-first design: big visuals + simple language match a kindergarten audience perfectly. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: A black-and-white scientific diagram with no labels
answers.feedback: ❌ No engagement, no warmth, and no help reading — totally mismatched to a kindergarten audience.

questions.text: The MAIN reason designers create a storyboard before opening any digital software is:

answers.text: Storyboards are required by school rules
answers.feedback: ❌ Storyboards aren't required by rules — smart designers choose them because they save time and effort.

answers.text: Sketches are cheap to change; finished video work is expensive to redo
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! That's why every studio in the world uses storyboards: catch problems while changes still cost seconds, not hours. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Storyboards look prettier than the final project
answers.feedback: ❌ Storyboards are usually rough on purpose. The point is planning, not beauty.

answers.text: Storyboards always have to be in color
answers.feedback: ❌ Storyboards are typically pencil sketches with notes. Color isn't required at this stage.

questions.text: Integration in multimedia design means:

answers.text: Adding more ingredients than necessary
answers.feedback: ❌ More isn't better — integration is about how the parts work together, not how many you have.

answers.text: Using exactly the same color throughout
answers.feedback: ❌ That's one tiny aspect of style. Integration is bigger — all ingredients supporting one idea.

answers.text: When all the ingredients (text, visuals, audio) support the same idea instead of fighting each other
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Integrated work feels coherent — every ingredient says the same thing. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Removing all images so only text remains
answers.feedback: ❌ That's not integration — that's deletion. Integration keeps the ingredients but makes them work together.

questions.text: Aesthetic unity in a multimedia project means:

answers.text: Every page uses different colors and fonts to keep things interesting
answers.feedback: ❌ The opposite! Variety on every page kills unity. The whole point is consistent choices across pages.

answers.text: Including as many colors and fonts as possible
answers.feedback: ❌ More isn't better. Aesthetic unity comes from RESTRAINT — a small fixed palette and font pair.

answers.text: Every page feels like part of the same project — same colors, same fonts, same layout style
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Aesthetic unity is the visual signal that one designer made one project. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Using the most expensive design software available
answers.feedback: ❌ Tools don't create unity. Discipline does — you can make unified work in any tool, even free ones.

questions.text: The recommended size of a project color palette is:

answers.text: At least 10 colors, the more the better
answers.feedback: ❌ Too many colors creates visual chaos. Real designers keep palettes small.

answers.text: Exactly 1 color
answers.feedback: ❌ One color is too restrictive — you can't show emphasis, backgrounds, or accents.

answers.text: About 3–5 colors used consistently across the project
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! 3–5 colors is the sweet spot — enough variety to show emphasis, few enough to feel unified. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: A new color for every page
answers.feedback: ❌ A new palette per page is the opposite of aesthetic unity.

questions.text: Which is the STRONGEST piece of peer feedback?

answers.text: "Good job!"
answers.feedback: ❌ Vague — your classmate doesn't know what to keep doing or how to improve.

answers.text: "On page 2, the text is hard to read against the photo — could you add a darker background behind the words?"
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Specific (names the page and problem), kind (offers a solution), and actionable. Classic strong Glow/Grow. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: "It's bad."
answers.feedback: ❌ Vague AND unkind. Tells your classmate nothing useful.

answers.text: "Change everything."
answers.feedback: ❌ Overwhelming and not specific. Strong feedback names ONE thing at a time.

questions.text: You and a teammate are co-editing a Canva project. You disagree with their photo choice. The BEST first action is:

answers.text: Silently delete and replace the photo with your own choice
answers.feedback: ❌ Silently overwriting a teammate's work breaks trust. Always communicate first.

answers.text: Stop working on the project
answers.feedback: ❌ Quitting on a small disagreement is unfair to your teammate and the work.

answers.text: Leave a Canva comment explaining your concern and suggesting an alternative
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Comments protect collaboration. They give your teammate a chance to respond before changes happen. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: Tell the teacher first before talking to your teammate
answers.feedback: ❌ Save the teacher for big issues. Small disagreements are best handled inside the team using comments.

questions.text: The 6th item on the FINAL QUALITY CHECKLIST asks you to confirm:

answers.text: Page count is at least 10
answers.feedback: ❌ More pages doesn't mean better. Page count isn't on the checklist.

answers.text: Background music is exactly 30 seconds
answers.feedback: ❌ Music length isn't a checklist item. Integration covers whether music FITS the project.

answers.text: Every collaborator is credited and any borrowed images or sounds are attributed
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Honest credit (justice in action) and attribution of borrowed work are non-negotiable for honest design. (SC.6.CC.2.1)

answers.text: The project took at least one week to make
answers.feedback: ❌ Time isn't a checklist item. A great project is great whether it took 30 minutes or 3 weeks.

questions.text: A file extension (like .docx or .mp3) tells the computer:

answers.text: .stl

answers.text: .mp4

answers.text: .pdf

answers.text: .stl

quizzes.title: Week 9 Quiz — The Journey of Data

questions.text: A song file is sitting on your phone, untouched, in your music folder. Which state is that data in?

answers.text: Data in motion
answers.feedback: ❌ Data in motion is traveling across a network. The song file isn't moving — it's just stored.

answers.text: Data at rest
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Data at rest means stored on a device and not actively moving or being processed. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: Data in use
answers.feedback: ❌ Data in use means open in an app and being read or processed. The file is not open right now.

answers.text: Data in transit
answers.feedback: ❌ "In transit" is another way to describe data in motion — but the song isn't moving. It's at rest.

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST example of cloud storage?

answers.text: A USB stick plugged into your laptop
answers.feedback: ❌ A USB stick is local storage — it lives on your physical device.

answers.text: The hard drive built into a desktop computer
answers.feedback: ❌ A built-in hard drive is local storage — it sits inside the computer itself.

answers.text: A Google Drive folder you can open from any device with internet
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Cloud storage lives on a remote server you reach over the internet — Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud, and Dropbox are all examples. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: An SD card inside a digital camera
answers.feedback: ❌ An SD card is local storage — a tiny chip that lives in the device.

questions.text: Your home Wi-Fi connects your laptop, phone, and smart TV — all in your house. What kind of network is that?

answers.text: WAN (Wide Area Network)
answers.feedback: ❌ A WAN connects networks across cities, states, or countries. A home network is much smaller.

answers.text: LAN (Local Area Network)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A LAN connects devices in one place — like a single home, school, or office. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: A database
answers.feedback: ❌ A database is an organized collection of data — not a type of network.

answers.text: A server farm
answers.feedback: ❌ A server farm is a building full of servers, not the kind of network in your house.

questions.text: What is the main job of a server?

answers.text: To send Wi-Fi signals around your house
answers.feedback: ❌ That's a router or wireless access point — not a server.

answers.text: To store data and serve it to many users at once
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A server is a powerful computer built to serve data to many users at the same time. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: To translate languages on the internet
answers.feedback: ❌ Translation apps do that — not servers as a whole.

answers.text: To plug in printers and external mice
answers.feedback: ❌ USB hubs and ports do that. A server's job is much bigger — storing and delivering data to many users.

questions.text: You search Canvas for the words "ancient Rome." Your search words become a request that the app sends to a database. What is that request called?

answers.text: A query
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A query is a request that tells a database what data to find and return. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: A packet
answers.feedback: ❌ A packet is a small chunk of data traveling on a network — not a search instruction.

answers.text: A LAN
answers.feedback: ❌ A LAN is a Local Area Network — not a search request.

answers.text: A server
answers.feedback: ❌ A server is the computer that stores or delivers data — not the question you ask it.

questions.text: You want your dad to read your essay but NOT change any of your sentences. Which role should you give him?

answers.text: Owner
answers.feedback: ❌ Owner has full control — including delete and re-share. Way more than needed for "just read it."

answers.text: Editor
answers.feedback: ❌ Editor can change your sentences. You said you don't want him doing that.

answers.text: Viewer
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Viewer is read-only — he can open and read but cannot change anything. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Commenter
answers.feedback: ❌ Commenter could leave comments on your file. If you only want him to read silently, Viewer is the tighter choice.

questions.text: Your teacher wants to leave feedback on your draft but should NOT rewrite your sentences. Which role gives her exactly what she needs?

answers.text: Editor
answers.feedback: ❌ Editor can rewrite your sentences directly. The question said she shouldn't.

answers.text: Viewer
answers.feedback: ❌ Viewer is read-only — she couldn't leave feedback at all.

answers.text: Commenter
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Commenter can read and leave comments or suggestions, but cannot change the actual content. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Owner
answers.feedback: ❌ Owner has full control of the file, including delete. Far too much access for a feedback role.

questions.text: What is the principle of least privilege?

answers.text: Always give every user the highest possible role so nothing breaks
answers.feedback: ❌ That's the OPPOSITE of least privilege — and a recipe for accidents and leaks.

answers.text: Give every user exactly the access they need to do their job — and nothing more
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Match the role to the real need — no extra access. The fewer keys floating around, the safer your data. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Only the IT admin should ever have access to anything
answers.feedback: ❌ That would block real work. Least privilege means right-sizing access, not eliminating it.

answers.text: Default to "Anyone with the link" so people don't have to ask
answers.feedback: ❌ That's the most-privilege setting, not least privilege. It's the kind of mistake that causes real-world data leaks.

questions.text: Which sharing setting is the MOST risky for a private file you don't want strangers to see?

answers.text: Specific people, role: Viewer
answers.feedback: ❌ Very safe — only the people you list can find it, and they can only read.

answers.text: Anyone in your school, role: Viewer
answers.feedback: ❌ Some risk, since everyone in your school can find it — but the public still can't.

answers.text: Anyone with the link, role: Editor
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The most dangerous combo — anyone who gets the link can not only read but also change your file. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Specific people, role: Editor
answers.feedback: ❌ Reasonable for a small trusted group — only the named people can find it, even if they can edit.

questions.text: Your sister leaves her laptop open and signed into her email. You see a private message from her teacher about her grades. What is the right thing to do?

answers.text: Read the message — her email is right there in front of you
answers.feedback: ❌ Just because you CAN see it doesn't mean you SHOULD. That's the whole idea of ethical access.

answers.text: Look away, close the laptop, and let her know it was open
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Treat other people's private data the way you'd want them to treat yours — close the door and walk away. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Read it and screenshot it, in case it's useful later
answers.feedback: ❌ Even worse — now you've made a copy of someone else's private data without permission.

answers.text: Reply to the teacher on her behalf to be helpful
answers.feedback: ❌ You'd be impersonating her — and using her account without permission. Big trust break.

quizzes.title: Week 11 Quiz — Phishing, Social Engineering & Privacy

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST definition of phishing?

answers.text: A type of fishing app for your phone
answers.feedback: ❌ Phishing is NOT a real fishing app — the spelling comes from a hacker term, but it's a scam, not a sport.

answers.text: A scam that uses fake messages to trick people into giving up passwords or personal info
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Phishing uses fake messages — emails, texts, DMs — to trick people into handing over secret info. (SC.6.CS.1.3)

answers.text: A virus that damages computer hardware
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes a hardware-damaging virus. Phishing tricks PEOPLE — not the hardware itself.

answers.text: A way to back up your files to the cloud
answers.feedback: ❌ That's cloud backup — a totally different topic and not a scam.

questions.text: Which piece of information should be classified as CONFIDENTIAL — never shared with anyone online, no matter who claims to be asking?

answers.text: Your favorite music genre
answers.feedback: ❌ Music tastes are PUBLIC — totally fine to share.

answers.text: The name of your school
answers.feedback: ❌ A school name is generally PUBLIC — printed on jerseys, posted on websites.

answers.text: Your password and the 6-digit MFA code that just texted to your phone
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Passwords and MFA codes are CONFIDENTIAL. Real companies will NEVER ask for them — anyone who does is trying to scam you. (SC.6.CS.1.4)

answers.text: Your favorite sports team
answers.feedback: ❌ Sports preferences are PUBLIC — already visible on your profile or already known.

questions.text: Which of these is the STRONGEST password?

answers.text: password123
answers.feedback: ❌ One of the most common passwords in the world. A computer cracks it in under a second.

answers.text: qwerty
answers.feedback: ❌ The top 5 letters on a keyboard. Computers try this in their first 100 guesses.

answers.text: orange-lamp-tiger-cloud-9
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A long passphrase with random words and a number is hard to guess and would take longer than the age of the universe to brute-force. (SC.6.CS.2.1)

answers.text: your first name + the year you were born
answers.feedback: ❌ Way too easy to guess if a phisher knows even a little about you. Avoid name + birthdate combos.

questions.text: What does multi-factor authentication (MFA) protect you against, even if a scammer steals your password?

answers.text: Slow internet speeds
answers.feedback: ❌ MFA isn't about speed — it's about identity.

answers.text: Account takeover by an attacker who has only your password
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Even if a phisher steals your password, they can't log in without the second factor (a code on your phone). (SC.6.CS.2.1)

answers.text: Lost device damage and broken screens
answers.feedback: ❌ MFA doesn't protect physical devices — it protects access to your accounts.

answers.text: Battery drain on your phone
answers.feedback: ❌ MFA has nothing to do with battery life.

questions.text: You're at a coffee shop on free public Wi-Fi. Which activity is the LEAST safe to do on this network?

answers.text: Reading a public news article
answers.feedback: ❌ Reading public news is low-risk on any network — you're not exposing private credentials.

answers.text: Watching a YouTube video
answers.feedback: ❌ Watching public videos is low-risk — no private logins involved.

answers.text: Logging into your bank account and transferring money
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Banking and other sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi can be intercepted. Wait until you're on a trusted network. (SC.6.HS.1.1)

answers.text: Checking the weather
answers.feedback: ❌ Looking up public info isn't risky. The danger is logging into accounts with sensitive data.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of encryption?

answers.text: To make data load faster on the internet
answers.feedback: ❌ Encryption isn't about speed — it adds a small bit of work, not less.

answers.text: To scramble a message so only the right person can read it
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext that's unreadable without the key. (SC.6.CS.1.5)

answers.text: To delete old messages automatically
answers.feedback: ❌ Encryption doesn't delete anything — it scrambles messages so only the right person can read them.

answers.text: To store data permanently in the cloud
answers.feedback: ❌ That's cloud storage. Encryption is about protecting messages, not where they live.

questions.text: Using a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3, what does the ciphertext FDW decrypt to (shift each letter back 3)?

answers.text: DOG
answers.feedback: ❌ Shift each letter back 3: F→C, D→A, W→T = CAT, not DOG.

answers.text: CAT
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! F→C, D→A, W→T. The plaintext is CAT. (SC.6.CS.1.5)

answers.text: BAT
answers.feedback: ❌ Close, but B is shift-back 4 from F. With shift 3, F goes back to C — so the answer starts with C, not B.

answers.text: CAR
answers.feedback: ❌ First two letters are right (CA), but W shifts back 3 to T — not R.

questions.text: What does the "s" in https:// tell you about a website connection?

answers.text: It means the site is faster than other sites
answers.feedback: ❌ The "s" has nothing to do with speed. It stands for SECURE.

answers.text: It means the connection is encrypted (secure) so data is scrambled while it travels
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! HTTPS means encryption is protecting the connection. Without HTTPS, your password would travel as plaintext. (SC.6.CS.1.5)

answers.text: It means the site is owned by the school
answers.feedback: ❌ The "s" doesn't say anything about who owns the site — it's about encryption.

answers.text: Nothing — http and https are exactly the same
answers.feedback: ❌ HTTPS and HTTP are very different. HTTPS is encrypted; HTTP is plaintext. The "s" makes a big difference.

questions.text: Which of these is the SAFEST username for a public game leaderboard?

answers.text: SophiaMartinez_2014
answers.feedback: ❌ Real first name + last name + birth year is way too much PII for a public profile.

answers.text: SophiaM_OakRidgeMS
answers.feedback: ❌ Real name + the school you attend is enough for a stranger to find you in real life.

answers.text: BlueDragon42
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Memorable, but no real name, school, or birthday — keeps your identity private. (SC.6.CS.1.6)

answers.text: 7thGrade_Rm104_Sophia

questions.text: Which of these is an example of a PASSIVE digital footprint — data collected automatically, not posted by you on purpose?

answers.text: A discussion-board reply you typed
answers.feedback: ❌ That's an ACTIVE footprint — you wrote and posted it on purpose.

answers.text: A photo you uploaded to your profile
answers.feedback: ❌ Active — you chose to upload it.

answers.text: A list of YouTube videos you've watched, tracked by the app
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! You didn't post your watch history — the app collected it automatically. That's a passive footprint. (SC.6.CS.1.6)

answers.text: A bio sentence you wrote on your profile
answers.feedback: ❌ Active — those words went up because you typed them.

questions.text: What does the "A" for Authority in the CRAAP test ask you to check?

answers.text: When the article was last updated
answers.feedback: ❌ That's CURRENCY (the first C in CRAAP), not Authority.

answers.text: Whether the article fits your specific question
answers.feedback: ❌ That's RELEVANCE — the R in CRAAP.

answers.text: Who wrote it and what makes them an expert
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Authority asks about the AUTHOR — their name, credentials, and qualification to write on the topic. (SC.6.HS.1.2)

answers.text: Why the website exists in the first place
answers.feedback: ❌ That's PURPOSE — the P in CRAAP.

questions.text: Which top-level domain (TLD) is restricted only to U.S. government agencies?

answers.text: .com
answers.feedback: ❌ Anyone can register a .com — it's the most open TLD on the internet.

answers.text: .org
answers.feedback: ❌ Originally for non-profits, but now anyone can register .org.

answers.text: .gov
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Only U.S. government agencies can use .gov — like nasa.gov, usa.gov, weather.gov. (SC.6.HS.1.2)

answers.text: .edu
answers.feedback: ❌ .edu is restricted, but to U.S. accredited SCHOOLS (universities and some K-12), not to the government.

questions.text: What is lateral reading?

answers.text: Reading the same article over and over until you remember it
answers.feedback: ❌ Re-reading the same page doesn't fact-check it — you need OTHER sources for that.

answers.text: Leaving the page to fact-check it on other trusted sources
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Lateral reading means leaving the page and searching what other trusted sources say about the site or claim. Fact-checkers use this all the time. (SC.6.HS.1.2)

answers.text: Reading by holding the screen sideways
answers.feedback: ❌ Lateral reading isn't about screen orientation — it's about checking sources against each other.

answers.text: Skipping every other paragraph to save time
answers.feedback: ❌ That's skim-reading. Lateral reading means cross-checking with OTHER sources.

questions.text: A pop-up screams: "YOUR COMPUTER IS INFECTED — call 1-800-FAKE-NOW immediately!" What is the BEST move?

answers.text: Call the number to fix the problem
answers.feedback: ❌ Real Microsoft and Apple NEVER show pop-ups asking you to call a phone number. The pop-up itself is the scam.

answers.text: Pay them with a gift card so they help faster
answers.feedback: ❌ Gift-card payment to "tech support" is a flashing-red sign of a scam. Real companies don't take gift cards.

answers.text: Close the pop-up; don't call. If it won't close, force-quit the browser and tell a trusted adult.
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Fake tech support pop-ups are common scams. Close, don't call, and ask a trusted adult if it won't close. (SC.6.HS.1.4)

answers.text: Click through every option in the pop-up to find a "decline" button
answers.feedback: ❌ Clicking through pop-ups often installs malware. Don't engage — just close.

questions.text: You're writing a 6th-grade report on the history of NASA. Which is the BEST source to cite?

answers.text: An anonymous fan blog with no dates and no citations
answers.feedback: ❌ No author, no dates, no citations — that fails most of CRAAP.

answers.text: A YouTube comment thread arguing about space
answers.feedback: ❌ Comments aren't sources — no author, no facts, no review.

answers.text: nasa.gov — NASA's own official .gov website
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! NASA's own .gov website is a primary source — high authority on its own programs and citation-quality. (SC.6.HS.1.2)

answers.feedback: ❌ Pinterest re-shares images without source info. Not citation-quality.

answers.feedback: ❌ Endless scrolling is the textbook example of PASSIVE screen time, not active.

answers.text: Watching reaction videos auto-play in the background
answers.feedback: ❌ Background auto-play is the most passive form of screen use.

answers.text: Coding a small project or video-calling Grandma
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Coding (creating) and video-calling (genuinely connecting) are textbook active screen time. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Falling asleep with a movie on
answers.feedback: ❌ That's passive — and combined with sleep disruption, it's a wellness double-whammy.

questions.text: Why does using your phone in bed at night make it harder to fall asleep?

answers.text: The phone is too heavy to hold for long
answers.feedback: ❌ Phone weight isn't the issue. The issue is light affecting your sleep hormones.

answers.text: Blue light from the screen suppresses melatonin and tells your brain it's daytime
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Blue light suppresses melatonin and pushes back the sleep signal in your brain. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Phones drain the oxygen in your room
answers.feedback: ❌ Phones don't change room oxygen. The mechanism is light, not air.

answers.text: Apps secretly broadcast caffeine
answers.feedback: ❌ Not a real thing. The real mechanism is blue-light suppression of melatonin.

questions.text: What does the 20-20-20 rule recommend for digital eye strain?

answers.text: Use 20 different apps every 20 minutes
answers.feedback: ❌ App-switching has nothing to do with eye strain. The rule is about distance breaks.

answers.text: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Quick distance breaks every 20 minutes give your eye muscles a chance to relax. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Limit yourself to 20 minutes of screen time per day
answers.feedback: ❌ The rule isn't a daily total — it's a break schedule for whatever screen time you DO have.

answers.text: Look at a screen for 20 hours and then take 20 minutes off
answers.feedback: ❌ That's way too much screen time. The rule is much smaller and more frequent.

answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Doomscrolling is reading bad news after bad news, often late at night, leaving you anxious about things that aren't actually happening to you. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.feedback: ❌ Scroll speed has nothing to do with the term. It's about WHAT you scroll, not HOW fast.

answers.text: A built-in phone setting that locks your screen
answers.feedback: ❌ Doomscrolling is a behavior, not a phone setting.

questions.text: Which is the BEST habit for keeping your phone from wrecking your sleep?

answers.text: "I'll try to use my phone less at night"
answers.feedback: ❌ That's a wish, not a habit. Vague intentions rarely change behavior.

answers.text: Plug your phone in across the room at 9 p.m. and use a real alarm clock
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Concrete, specific, and removes the temptation. That's how habits actually stick. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Sleep with your phone under your pillow but try not to check it
answers.feedback: ❌ If the phone is right there, you'll check it. Distance is the whole point.

answers.feedback: ❌ Better than face-up, but the phone is still right there to grab. Across-the-room is the stronger habit.

answers.feedback: ❌ That would block real work. Least privilege means right-sizing access, not eliminating it.

answers.feedback: ❌ That's the most-privilege setting, not least privilege.

answers.feedback: ❌ That's data AT REST — stored on a device and not moving.

questions.text: You're heading to a remote campsite for a week with no Wi-Fi or cell signal. You want to listen to 50 of your favorite songs. Which storage choice makes the most sense?

answers.text: Stream the songs from a cloud music service
answers.feedback: ❌ Streaming needs an internet connection — which you won't have at the campsite.

answers.text: Save the songs in cloud storage like Google Drive
answers.feedback: ❌ Cloud storage also needs internet to reach the files. Same problem as streaming.

answers.text: Download the songs to local storage on your phone
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Local storage works without internet. Once they're on your device, you can play them anywhere. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: Email the songs to yourself before you leave
answers.feedback: ❌ Even if the email arrived, you'd still need internet to open the attachments.

questions.text: A school district has five separate campuses, all sharing one student-records system. Which type of network connects the campuses?

answers.text: LAN (Local Area Network)
answers.feedback: ❌ A LAN connects devices in ONE place — like a single building. Five separate campuses are too far apart.

answers.text: WAN (Wide Area Network)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A WAN connects multiple LANs across cities, states, or countries — like a five-campus district. (SC.6.CS.1.1)

answers.text: A USB connection
answers.feedback: ❌ USB connects two devices physically. It can't reach across multiple campuses.

answers.text: A database
answers.feedback: ❌ A database is an organized collection of data — not a type of network.

questions.text: You finish a personal essay and want your dad to read it but NOT change any of your sentences. Which role should you give him?

answers.text: Owner
answers.feedback: ❌ Owner has full control — including delete and re-share. Way more than needed for "just read it."

answers.text: Editor
answers.feedback: ❌ Editor can change your sentences. You said you don't want him doing that.

answers.text: Viewer
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Viewer is read-only — he can open and read but cannot change anything. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.text: Commenter
answers.feedback: ❌ Commenter could leave comments on your file. If you only want him to read silently, Viewer is the tighter choice.

questions.text: Which sharing setting is the MOST RISKY for a private file you don't want strangers to see?

answers.text: Anyone in your school, role: Viewer
answers.feedback: ❌ Some risk, since everyone in your school can find it — but the public still can't.

answers.text: Anyone with the link, role: Editor
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The most dangerous combo — anyone who gets the link can not only read but also change your file. (SC.6.CS.1.2)

answers.feedback: ❌ Reasonable for a small trusted group — only the named people can find it, even if they can edit.

questions.text: Using a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3, what does the ciphertext FDW decrypt to (shift each letter back 3)?

answers.text: DOG
answers.feedback: ❌ Shift each letter back 3: F→C, D→A, W→T = CAT, not DOG.

answers.text: CAT
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! F→C, D→A, W→T. The plaintext is CAT. (SC.6.CS.1.5)

answers.text: BAT
answers.feedback: ❌ Close, but B is shift-back 4 from F. With shift 3, F goes back to C — so the answer starts with C, not B.

answers.text: CAR
answers.feedback: ❌ First two letters are right (CA), but W shifts back 3 to T — not R.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of a PASSIVE digital footprint — data collected automatically, not posted by you on purpose?

answers.text: A discussion-board reply you typed
answers.feedback: ❌ That's an ACTIVE footprint — you wrote and posted it on purpose.

answers.text: A photo you uploaded to your profile
answers.feedback: ❌ Active — you chose to upload it.

answers.text: A list of YouTube videos you've watched, tracked by the app
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! You didn't post your watch history — the app collected it automatically. That's a passive footprint. (SC.6.CS.1.6)

answers.text: A bio sentence you wrote on your profile
answers.feedback: ❌ Active — those words went up because you typed them.

questions.text: Which top-level domain (TLD) is restricted only to U.S. government agencies?

answers.text: .com
answers.feedback: ❌ Anyone can register a .com — it's the most open TLD.

answers.text: .org
answers.feedback: ❌ Originally for non-profits, but now anyone can register .org.

answers.text: .gov
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Only U.S. government agencies can use .gov — like nasa.gov, usa.gov, weather.gov. (SC.6.HS.1.2)

answers.text: .edu
answers.feedback: ❌ .edu is restricted to U.S. accredited SCHOOLS, not the government.

questions.text: A pop-up screams: "YOUR COMPUTER IS INFECTED — call 1-800-FAKE-NOW immediately!" What is the BEST move?

answers.text: Call the number to fix the problem
answers.feedback: ❌ Real Microsoft and Apple NEVER show pop-ups asking you to call a phone number. The pop-up itself is the scam.

answers.text: Close the pop-up; don't call. If it won't close, force-quit the browser and tell a trusted adult.
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Fake tech-support pop-ups are common scams. Close, don't call, and ask a trusted adult if it won't close. (SC.6.HS.1.4)

answers.text: Pay them with a gift card so they help faster
answers.feedback: ❌ Gift-card payment to "tech support" is a flashing-red sign of a scam. Real companies don't take gift cards.

answers.text: Click through every option in the pop-up
answers.feedback: ❌ Clicking through pop-ups often installs malware. Don't engage — just close.

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST example of active screen time?

answers.text: Endlessly scrolling Reels and Shorts
answers.feedback: ❌ Endless scrolling is the textbook example of PASSIVE screen time, not active.

answers.text: Watching reaction videos auto-play in the background
answers.feedback: ❌ Background auto-play is the most passive form of screen use.

answers.text: Coding a small project or video-calling Grandma
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Coding (creating) and video-calling (genuinely connecting) are textbook active screen time. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Falling asleep with a movie on
answers.feedback: ❌ That's passive — and combined with sleep disruption, a wellness double-whammy.

questions.text: Why does using your phone in bed at night make it harder to fall asleep?

answers.text: The phone is too heavy to hold for long
answers.feedback: ❌ Phone weight isn't the issue. The issue is light affecting your sleep hormones.

answers.text: Blue light from the screen suppresses melatonin and tells your brain it's daytime
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Blue light suppresses melatonin and pushes back the sleep signal in your brain. (SC.6.HS.2.2)

answers.text: Phones drain the oxygen in your room
answers.feedback: ❌ Phones don't change room oxygen. The mechanism is light, not air.

answers.text: Apps secretly broadcast caffeine
answers.feedback: ❌ Not a real thing. The real mechanism is blue-light suppression of melatonin.
